original_question: Let X/C be a quasi-projective variety, let f : X → X be a morphism, let P ∈ X be a point, and let Y ⊆ X be a subvariety of X. Then {n ≥ 0 : f n (P ) ∈ Y } is a finite union of arithmetic progressions.
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the exact mathematical core of the paper’s formal statement almost verbatim: the ambient field is C, X is a quasi-projective variety, f is a self-morphism of X, P is an arbitrary point of X, Y is a subvariety of X, and the hitting-time set {n≥0 : f^n(P)∈Y} is asserted to be a finite union of arithmetic progressions.
missing_details: In the paper this is stated as an open conjecture, not a theorem in full generality: it is Conjecture 7.1, the Dynamical Mordell–Lang Conjecture.
The paper explicitly defines an arithmetic progression in N to mean a one-sided set {ak+b : k=0,1,2,...} with integers a,b≥0; it also allows a=0, so singleton sets are included.
For a fully stand-alone formulation, f^n should be identified as the n-th iterate of f, with the convention f^0=id_X coming from the notation section.
The surrounding discussion initially motivates the problem using a wandering point P, but the formal conjecture itself imposes no wandering hypothesis; P is arbitrary.
If orbit notation is used, the paper’s nearby notation is O_f(P)={f^n(P): n≥0}.
refined_question: Dynamical Mordell–Lang Conjecture: Is it true that for every quasi-projective variety X over C, every morphism f:X→X, every point P∈X, and every subvariety Y⊆X, the set {n≥0 : f^n(P)∈Y}, where f^n denotes the n-th iterate of f, is a finite union of one-sided arithmetic progressions in N, i.e. sets of the form {ak+b : k=0,1,2,...} with integers a,b≥0, allowing a=0?
justification: The draft is targeting exactly the official Dynamical Mordell–Lang statement in the survey. The paper’s precise formulation appears in Section 7 as Conjecture 7.1. The sentence immediately before it supplies the paper’s exact meaning of arithmetic progression, Section 2 supplies the iterate/orbit notation, Definition 7.2 gives the nearby periodic/preperiodic-subvariety language used to explain consequences of the conjecture, Theorem 7.3 records two major proven cases, and Remark 7.7 identifies this as the dynamical analogue of the classical Mordell–Lang problem.
